newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Portuguese banks among Europe's most innovative.
newsitem.headline: Portuguese banks among Europe's most innovative.

text.p: Portugal's banking system is among the most innovative in Europe and the Portuguese are proving receptive to the new high-tech services on offer, a senior industry official said.

Portugal, one of the poorer nations in the European Union, was a late starter in absorbing banking technology but has quickly caught up with its more developed partners, said Filipe Dos Santos, Director General of Sociedade Interbancaria de Servicos (SIBS), which operates the country's cashpoint system.
He told Reuters in an interview that Portugal matched Belgium, a more developed society with a similar population, in terms of the number of electronic banking transactions per head.
"We are applying innovation to technology that other European countries already have but perhaps do not use as extensively as we do," Dos Santos said late on Tuesday.
"Cashpoints are popular across Europe. But in Portugal they provide an ample, varied range of services that in general is not found in other European countries," he added.

On Tuesday SIBS, a private company owned by 30 banks, and mobile phone operator Telecel launched a new service called "Telemultibanco" permitting Telecel's 200,000 customers to pay bills and check bank account balances using their mobile phones.
Unlike in other European countries, customers do not speak to a telephone operator and do not need to make prior arrangement with banks to pay specific bills, Dos Santos said.
They simply use a personal identification number (PIN) and conduct their transactions for the cost of a local phone call.
Customers will save time by avoiding queues at cash point machines. And banks will save money by providing a more efficient service that reduces paperwork.
Some 7.5 million banking cards exist in Portugal, whose population is 10 million. The Portuguese widely use debit cards at "Multibanco" cash points to pay bills and withdraw cash.
Dos Santos said nothing prevented mobile phone operator TMN-Telecommunicacoes Moveis Nacionais from following its main rival Telecel and eventually launching its own Telemultibanco.

Portuguese banking has taken other innovative steps recently, such as the introduction of the "Porta Moedas", a banking card accepted widely by retail outlets which allows customers to make small transactions instead of using cash.
Customers deposit as much money as they need in their Porta Moedas account, enabling them to make small transactions such as pay for a taxi ride or buy a newspaper.
Banco Portugues do Atlantico has unmanned outlets where customers carry out a range of routine transactions.
A recently established unit of Banco Comercial Portugues, Banco Sete, offers telephone banking services.
Unlike in other European countries where customers may be distrustful of high-tech banking services, the Portuguese are receptive to the new technology, Dos Santos said.
"There is confidence among the general public," he said. "Our analysis is that the new services are very secure."
While Dos Santos was optimistic about the Telemultibanco and Porta Moedas, he said telephone banking was conducted mainly by companies and wealthy individuals in Portugal.
"Home banking" had not really caught on as banks had not marketed the service aggressively and few Portuguese owned personal computers with modems.
Dos Santos estimated that some 20,000-30,000 Portuguese owned computers while as many as 400,000 owned mobile phones.
